title: Space-Time Trade-Offs
summary: Deliberately spending memory to buy speed: memoization, precomputed lookup tables, and hashing as an explicit, namable interview lever rather than an accident of how code happens to be written.

slides.markdown:
Most of this group has been about measuring complexity that's already there. This topic is about **choosing** it: deliberately spending extra memory to make an algorithm faster, as an explicit design lever rather than a side effect.

The pattern shows up in three closely related forms: **memoization** (cache a subproblem's result so you never recompute it), **precomputed lookup tables** (pay the cost once, up front, so every query afterward is O(1)), and **hashing** (spend memory on a hash table in exchange for O(1) average lookups instead of O(n) scans).

All three are the same underlying trade: time drops, memory rises. Interviewers ask for this explicitly ("can you trade space for time here?") often enough that naming the lever by name — not just applying it — is part of what a strong answer sounds like.

**Memoization** caches the result of a function call keyed by its arguments, so that calling it again with the same arguments returns instantly instead of recomputing. It's the direct fix for exactly the problem `recursion-recurrences-and-the-recursion-tree` identified in naive Fibonacci: the recursion tree recomputes the same smaller subproblems an exponential number of times.

With a cache, `fib(5)` is computed once, stored, and every later call that needs `fib(5)` — and there are many, deep inside the tree — reads it back in O(1) instead of re-expanding the whole subtree beneath it. The exponential tree of recomputation collapses into a linear number of **distinct** subproblems, each solved exactly once.

The cost is memory: the cache itself grows to hold every distinct subproblem's result, which is why this is a *trade*, not a free win — you're spending O(n) space (one entry per distinct subproblem) to save an exponential amount of redundant time.

| Version | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Naive recursive Fibonacci | O(2ⁿ) | O(n) stack | recomputes every subproblem from scratch, exponentially many times |
| Memoized recursive Fibonacci | O(n) | O(n) cache + O(n) stack | each of the n distinct subproblems computed exactly once, then reused |

Same code shape — same recursive calls, same base case — with one addition: check the cache before recursing, and write to it before returning. That single change moves the time complexity from exponential to linear, at the cost of an additional O(n) of cache memory on top of the stack space that was already there.

This table is the concrete version of the abstract claim in the snapshot: the trade isn't hypothetical, it's this exact before/after, and it's one of the most common "optimize this" follow-ups in interviews precisely because the fix is small and the payoff is dramatic.

Memoization caches results **as they're discovered, during execution**. A **precomputed lookup table** goes further: compute every answer you might ever need **up front**, before any query arrives, and store them all — turning every future query into a single O(1) array or hashmap read.

The classic example: if you'll be asked "is n prime?" for many values of n up to some bound N, computing primality from scratch each time (trial division) costs O(√n) per query. Running a **sieve** once up front costs O(N log log N) total, and afterward every query is a single O(1) array lookup — a huge win if the number of queries is large relative to N.

The trade-off calculus here is explicitly about **query volume**: precomputing pays off when you'll answer many queries against the same fixed universe of possible inputs; it's wasted work if you only ever need one or two answers, where computing on demand is cheaper overall.

A hash table is itself a space-time trade: you pay for a backing array plus the overhead of hash function computation and collision handling (see `hash-table-mechanics`), in exchange for turning an O(n) linear scan into an O(1) average lookup.

That overhead is real and worth naming, not treating as free: a hash table with n entries typically uses noticeably more memory per entry than a plain array or list would, because it reserves extra capacity to keep its load factor low (usually well under 100% full) and stores each key alongside its value rather than relying on implicit position. Choosing a hashmap over a sorted array for lookups is exactly the same category of decision as choosing to memoize — you are consciously spending memory the naive approach wouldn't need, in exchange for a better time bound.

The reason this belongs in the same topic as memoization and lookup tables: all three are instances of one lever — **materialize more state than the minimum required, so future work is cheaper.**

slides.subTitle: Recompute every time vs cache everything
slides.markdown:
Every one of these techniques sits somewhere on a spectrum between two extremes: **recompute from scratch on every query** (minimum memory, maximum repeated work) and **cache/precompute everything possible** (maximum memory, minimum repeated work). Most real solutions sit in the middle: memoize only the subproblems actually reached, hash only the keys actually inserted, precompute only up to the bound actually needed.

The middle ground matters because full precomputation isn't always better — if you'll only ever query a tiny fraction of the possible input space, memoizing on demand (compute and cache only what's asked for) uses far less memory than precomputing every possible answer up front, for the same eventual per-query speed once something has been cached once.

slides.sectionTitle: "Just use a hash map" isn't free
slides.markdown:
A common shortcut in interviews: reaching for "I'll use a hash map for O(1) lookup" as if it were a strictly better upgrade with no cost, without naming what it actually costs.

What it costs, concretely: extra memory beyond the raw data (each entry stores a key and a value, plus the backing array is kept well under full to control collisions), the hash function's own compute cost per operation, and — for a language without ordered dict guarantees — loss of insertion order unless you specifically choose an ordered variant. None of this makes the trade a bad one; it usually is a good one. But naming the cost, not just the benefit, is exactly what separates "I'll use a hash map" from a considered trade-off answer.

The strongest version of this answer names the actual number when it matters: "O(n) extra space for the hash table, in exchange for O(1) average lookup instead of O(n) — worth it here since we do that lookup inside a loop."

The decision to trade space for time should be sized, not assumed. Two concrete scenarios that resolve differently:

- **A function called once, on one input of size n = 40.** Naive recursive Fibonacci at n = 40 does roughly 2^40 ≈ 10¹² calls — far too slow. Memoizing costs O(40) ≈ 40 cache entries to fix it entirely. Here the trade is overwhelmingly worth it: trivial memory for an astronomical time win.
- **A prime-checking function called exactly once, for n up to 10¹².** A sieve up to 10¹² would need roughly a terabyte of memory to precompute — completely impractical — while a single trial-division check (O(√n) ≈ 10⁶ operations) runs in a fraction of a second. Here precomputing everything is the wrong trade; computing on demand wins because the query volume doesn't justify the memory.

The general habit: before reaching for memoization or a lookup table, estimate roughly how many distinct subproblems or keys will actually exist, and roughly how many times each would otherwise be recomputed — that's the real cost-benefit, not a reflexive "caching is always good."

slides.sectionTitle: The reverse trade: recompute to save memory
slides.markdown:
The trade runs both directions. Sometimes memory is the scarce resource, and it's worth deliberately **recomputing** something instead of storing it — the mirror image of everything above.

A concrete instance: computing Fibonacci with two rolling variables instead of a full memoization array. Since `fib(n)` only ever needs `fib(n-1)` and `fib(n-2)`, keeping the full O(n) cache is unnecessary — two variables, updated each iteration, give the same O(n) time with **O(1)** space, discarding every earlier result the moment it's no longer needed. This is a common interview follow-up to a memoized solution: "can you do this in O(1) space?" — and the answer is almost always "only keep what the very next step actually needs, and throw the rest away."

Another instance: gradient checkpointing in deep learning deliberately **discards** intermediate activations during a forward pass and **recomputes** them during backpropagation, trading extra compute for a large reduction in GPU memory — the same lever, aimed at the opposite bottleneck.

A complete space-time trade-off answer names: **the lever** ("I'll memoize" / "I'll precompute a table" / "I'll hash instead of scan"), **the concrete before/after numbers** ("O(2ⁿ) time drops to O(n), at the cost of an O(n) cache"), and **why the trade is worth it here specifically** ("we'll call this function many times on overlapping subproblems, so the cache pays for itself quickly").

That last part is what separates a reflexive "I'll just cache it" from a genuinely senior answer — knowing the lever exists is table stakes; knowing when spending memory is and isn't the right call, and being able to size the trade with real numbers, is what this whole group has been building toward. From here, the complexity toolkit is complete: naming variables and cases, deriving Big-O mechanically from code or a recurrence, accounting for amortization and the call stack, and now choosing complexity deliberately rather than only measuring it.
